name: Callejón del Diablo and Callejón del Infierno
where: Two lanes just south of the Alcázar, by Calle del Cristo de la Calavera and the Plaza del Seco
text: Two lanes a few steps apart, just south of the Alcázar, carry the darkest names in Toledo: the Callejón del Diablo and the Callejón del Infierno, the Devil's Alley and Hell's Alley. Nobody knows for certain where the names came from. The stories say this corner of the city, around the little Plaza del Seco, was where witches and sorcerers met. One tale tells of a student who sold his soul here for forbidden knowledge, then tried to cheat the devil, who left the marks of his fire on the walls. On windy nights, they say, you can hear whispering between the stones.
source: OSM way 114290350 (Callejón El Diablo); Callejón El Infierno OSM way 113814611 (39.85718, -4.02217)

name: Virgen de los Alfileritos
where: A glass niche on Calle Alfileritos, a few steps from Zocodover
text: In a glass niche on this narrow lane, a few steps from Zocodover, stands a small Virgin among candles and flowers. The best-loved version of her legend tells of Doña Soledad de Vargas, a young woman who came here to pray for love. Each time she prayed, she pushed a pin through the little grille as her offering. Others say the pins were meant to bring an absent lover home. Either way, the custom never died: Toledans still leave a pin here when they ask for a sweetheart. Look closely and you will see them, bright in the candlelight.

name: The Cobertizos
where: Covered lanes around Santo Domingo el Real and Santa Clara, north of the old town
text: A cobertizo is a lane that runs under the houses, roofed over by rooms built across the street. These tunnels were the darkest places in the old city, and Toledans filled them with stories. Night walkers spoke of footsteps that followed and then stopped, of cloaked figures that vanished at the far arch, and of lovers who met here because no window could see them. Walk through slowly. At night the vaults swallow sound, and every footstep seems to arrive a little late.
source: OSM way 257808773, Cobertizo de Santo Domingo el Real, lane midpoint (COORDS.md x3)

name: Torreón del Baño de la Cava
where: Ruined tower by the river, just north of the San Martín bridge
text: This ruined tower by the Tagus is tied to the last Visigothic king, Rodrigo. Legend says he watched from a window as Florinda, called La Cava, bathed in the river here, and he took her by force. Her father, Count Julián, governor of Ceuta, swore revenge and opened the straits to the Muslim armies in 711. So, the story goes, Spain was lost for a bath. Historians doubt every word, and the tower is really part of an old bridge. But the name has stuck for a thousand years, and on dark nights the river here is very loud.

name: Arco de la Sangre
where: The arch on the east side of Plaza de Zocodover
text: The Arch of the Blood, on the east side of Zocodover, is an old Moorish gateway through the inner walls. It takes its name from a small chapel above it that held an image called the Christ of the Blood. A popular story says the condemned prayed here on their way to execution; no record confirms it. The chapel and its Christ were destroyed in the Civil War, and the arch was rebuilt afterwards. Cervantes sits in bronze at its foot. He knew Toledo well, and the city appears in his stories.
source: Wikipedia ES 'Arco de la Sangre' 39.85945833, -4.02095833; OSM way 113802085

name: Peña del Rey Moro
where: Granite outcrop on the hills across the river, south of the old town, near the Ermita del Valle
text: Across the river, on the hills to the south, near the hermitage of the Valle, a pile of granite boulders looks, from the right angle, like the bust of a man in a turban. This is the Peña del Rey Moro, the Rock of the Moorish King. The legend says a Moorish king besieged Toledo, could not take it, and asked to be buried on that high point, so that he would face the city forever. Historians find no record of any such burial. Tonight you will see only the dark ridge across the gorge, from the viewpoints on the south side of the old town.
source: OSM way 393277683 (Ermita del Valle); the rock itself is not in OSM/Wikipedia lookups

name: La Campana Gorda
where: In the cathedral's bell tower, at its west end
text: High in the cathedral's bell tower hangs the Campana Gorda, the Fat Bell, one of the largest bells in Spain, weighing around eighteen tonnes. It was cast in the seventeen fifties, and it is famous less for its voice than for its fate: it cracked almost as soon as it was hung, within two months according to one account. Toledans have told stories about it ever since, and a nineteenth-century serial was even named after it. It still hangs in the tower. Look up at the dark belfry tonight.
source: OSM node 4450389993 (Catedral Primada, west end); tower not separately geocoded

name: Santa María la Blanca
where: Calle de los Reyes Católicos, old Jewish quarter
text: Behind a plain wall on Calle de los Reyes Católicos is one of the oldest synagogues still standing in Europe, a forest of white horseshoe arches built around eight hundred years ago. After violence against Toledo's Jews it became a church, and took the name it still has, Saint Mary the White. Its legend is about the ground itself: the Jews of Toledo, it is said, laid the floor with earth brought from Jerusalem, so that they would pray on holy soil. No archaeologist has found proof. Tradition keeps the story anyway. At night you see only the gate and the wall.

name: San Juan de los Reyes
where: Calle de los Reyes Católicos, west side of the old town above the San Martín bridge
text: The monastery of San Juan de los Reyes was built by Ferdinand and Isabella as their great church in Toledo. On its outer walls hang rows of iron chains, and they are real: the chains of Christian captives freed from Moorish prisons in the war for Granada, hung here as offerings. At night, in the floodlights, they look like a warning. Bécquer came here often to draw, and in one of his tales the narrow street he took on his way here leads to a window, and a woman he never sees.

name: Posada de la Hermandad
where: Calle de la Hermandad, just east of the cathedral
text: This old building near the cathedral was the seat of the Santa Hermandad, the brotherhood that policed the roads of Castile, and its prison. The stories say its cellars held dungeons where prisoners were tortured, and that a well inside was used for executions. Visitors and staff have reported footsteps, voices and noises nobody can explain. It is closed at night, but its heavy doorway and barred windows face the street. Stand there a moment and listen.

name: Alcázar: the Jewess of Toledo
where: The royal fortress at the top of the old town
text: The Alcázar, the royal fortress on top of the hill, was home to the kings of Castile, and one of them left Toledo a sad legend. Medieval chronicles say King Alfonso the Eighth fell so deeply in love with a Jewish woman of Toledo that he shut himself away with her and forgot his kingdom. The nobles, in some versions urged on by the queen, broke in and killed her. The chronicles call her Fermosa, the beautiful; later poets and playwrights called her Raquel. It was written down long after the king's death, perhaps to explain his defeats. Nobody knows where she lived.
source: OSM way 83998985 (Alcázar de Toledo). The legend has no fixed place; pinned at the royal residence

name: Roman baths and Toledo underground
where: Plaza Amador de los Ríos, just off the main street between Zocodover and the cathedral
text: Under Plaza Amador de los Ríos lie the remains of Roman baths, one of many spaces hidden beneath Toledo's streets. The city sits on a honeycomb of cisterns, cellars, wells and caves, and every guide has a tunnel story: a secret passage from the cathedral to the Alcázar for moving treasure in wartime, a labyrinth opening from an old river gate, cellars that join house to house. Most have never been mapped, and some night tours take you down into a private cellar to tell them. The baths, at least, are real.
